beats.narration_text: Every explanation of distributed training starts with a diagram of GPUs in a row. Almost none of them tell you what is actually being split, or where the time goes. I'm Anjana.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself

props.command: Training a large model needs more memory than one GPU has, so the work gets split across several. But the split can happen in different ways, and the diagrams never say which. Can you show me what actually gets divided — the data, the model, or both — and where the time really goes?
output: the weights are the small part of the budget
every GPU added costs you a synchronisation
the real constraint is bandwidth, not compute

beats.narration_text: A seven-billion-parameter model in full precision takes around twenty-eight gigabytes just to store its weights. Add optimizer states, gradients, and activations, and you need over a hundred gigabytes — more than any single GPU's memory. Even if the model fits, training on a large dataset takes weeks on one device. Distributed training splits the work across multiple GPUs. The question is what gets split: the data, the model, or both.

props.sparkLine: The weights are the small part.

beats.narration_text: Data parallelism is the most common strategy. Every GPU holds a complete copy of the model. The training dataset is split into different mini-batches — each GPU processes its own batch independently. After the forward and backward passes, each GPU has computed gradients from its own slice of data. The gradients are then averaged across all GPUs so every copy of the model updates identically. The result: each GPU sees different data, but they all stay synchronized. Training time scales nearly linearly with the number of GPUs.

Averaging gradients across GPUs sounds simple, but the communication pattern matters. All-reduce is the standard approach. In a ring all-reduce, each GPU sends a chunk of its gradients to the next GPU in a ring. After enough rounds, every GPU holds the fully averaged result — without any single GPU acting as a bottleneck. The alternative — sending everything to one central node — creates a bandwidth chokepoint that gets worse with every GPU added. Ring all-reduce scales because each GPU sends and receives the same amount of data regardless of cluster size.

When the model itself is too large for one GPU, you split the model. Tensor parallelism divides individual layers — a single matrix multiply is split across GPUs, each computing part of the result. Pipeline parallelism splits by layer groups — GPU one runs the first twelve layers, GPU two runs the next twelve. The input passes through GPUs in sequence, like a pipeline. The problem: while GPU two waits for GPU one's output, it sits idle. Micro-batching reduces this bubble by overlapping multiple smaller batches at different stages.

props.sparkLine: Splitting the model costs idle time.
